stories.title: Fun, flowing, not yet flawless: Lakers' league-best offense still has room to improve
stories.summary: The Lakers lead the league in scoring and its starting lineup has the best rating of any five-player group, but the chemistry is still developing.
stories.detailText: Lakers coach JJ Redick chats with guard Luka Doncic during a break in the action against the Heat on Monday night at Crpyto.com Arena. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) Austin Reaves described it as “fun.” Luka Doncic called the Lakers ’ effortless-looking offense as “flowing.” And this is still the early stages of development for a team that brought in nine new players. Through eight games, the Lakers have the most dynamic offense in the NBA. Led by Doncic, the Lakers are second in scoring with 122.5 points per game and first in offensive rating with 121.9 points per 100 possessions. The starting lineup of Doncic, Reaves, Walker Kessler , Ziaire Williams and Matisse Thybulle has a league-best 135.5 offensive rating among five-man groups that have played at least 40 minutes together entering Wednesday’s game at Sacramento. “Everything’s as expected,” guard Quentin Grimes said Monday after the Lakers hung 138 points in a 21-point win over the Miami Heat . “Winning, everybody’s getting involved, everybody’s making the right play, getting a lot of assists.” The Lakers (6-2) had 39 assists against the Heat, the most during JJ Redick ’s head-coaching tenure. Doncic is on a historic scoring binge; he is the first Laker since Kobe Bryant in 2007 to have five consecutive games of 35 or more points. While putting up a seemingly ho-hum 42 points against Miami, he also had a season-high 13 assists. “It’s a really good offense that we’re playing right now,” Redick said. “And a lot of that, of course, is Doncic and what he’s able to do and bend the defense.” Doncic, the NBA’s leading scorer at 38.3 points per game, does his damage early. He typically plays all 12 minutes of the opening quarter and leads the league with 15 points a game in the first quarter. Once he gets his shot going, teams send double teams to force the ball out of his hands. That’s when Doncic can be particularly dangerous. Read more: Luka Doncic's 42-point effort carries Lakers past Giannis Antetokounmpo and Heat Doncic has always been lauded for his superior court vision. But the Lakers are still learning to see the same picture. The Lakers had 14 turnovers, including 11 from Doncic and Reaves, during a preseason game against the Denver Nuggets, who were aggressively trapping the Lakers’ ballhandlers. The Lakers threw away a 25-point second-quarter lead on Oct. 30 when the Golden State Warriors ratcheted up the ball pressure. Doncic’s five turnovers a game are the second most in the league, and Reaves is third with 4.6 turnovers per game. Some players are new to being on a team with guards who get blitzed nearly every play, Reaves said. It requires players to not only be comfortable making decisions to pass, drive or shoot, but they have to choose quickly. A moment’s hesitation gives away the four-on-three advantage created by the double-team. Redick praised Grimes’ ability to keep advantages by driving decisively. Forward Sandro Mamukelashvili is also great at it, Redick said, as is guard Collin Sexton , who knows no speed other than full. The Lakers have also finished their advantages with Thybulle and Williams making27 of 58 (46.6%) three-point attempts combined. “That’s the beauty of our team,” Williams said. “You could put different guys at different spots and everyone’s able to make a play. All our guys are just dynamic and versatile. And everyone just wants to make the right play. No one wants to only shoot, there’s no egos. And that’s the fun part about it, you know? We all love to see each other succeed.” Williams missed three games because of a sore left foot but returned Monday with nine points, two rebounds and two assists off the bench. When Jake LaRavia jumped into the starting lineup, the Lakers were just as effective offensively as their first-choice lineup. When Doncic, Reaves, Kessler, Thybulle and LaRavia are together, the Lakers’ 144.3 points per 100 possessions ranks first among lineups that have played at least 30 minutes. But numbers don’t normalize until about 250 minutes, Redick believes. “I think there’s always room for improvement,” he said Monday. The Lakers have the most room for improvement on the defensive side. Their defensive rating of 114 points allowed per 100 possessions is tied with the Clippers for 20th in the NBA. They still rank 28th in rebounding, despite three consecutive double-doubles from Kessler, who responded after Redick challenged the center to be a larger rebounding presence. “This team can become a great team,” Redick said before Monday’s win over the Heat. “That requires patience, that requires a lot of coaching and teaching and buy-in, and so that whole process takes time.” Sign up for our weekly newsletter on all things Lakers. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

stories.title: Seven players have 2027-28 rookie contract options declined
stories.summary: Another three players were outright waived by teams, while 19 had their options picked up.
stories.detailText: Missing in the first round of an NBA Draft is a setback in team building, but for seven teams this year it was better to accept the pain now rather than keep the player around for the final year of their rookie deal. Seven players did not have their rookie-scale team options for the 2027-28 season picked up, the deadline was Monday. Those players are (via Keith Smith of Spotrac), in order of most to least expensive deals declined: • Tidjane Salaun, Charlotte Hornets ($10.4 million) • Cody Williams, Minnesota Timberwolves ($7.6 million) • Nikola Topic, Oklahoma City Thunder ($7.5 million) • A.J. Johnson, New Orleans Pelicans ($5.5 million) • DaRon Holmes II, Denver Nuggets ($5.5 million) • Pacome Dadiet, New York Knicks ($5.4 million) • Isaiah Collier, Utah Jazz($4.8 million) Some of these were simply financial decisions in the apron era, such as Pacome Dadiet with the Knicks. Three players were outright waived by their teams before this season: • Rob Dillingham (waived by the Hornets after being traded for Buddy Hield, has yet to re-sign) • Dalton Knecht (waived by the Lakers, signed as a two-way player with the Knicks) • Devin Carter (waived by Hawks, signed as a two-way player by Celtics) There were 19 players who had their extensions picked up, they are extension-eligible next summer or could be headed to 2028 restricted free agency. Among those are Stephon Castle (Spurs), Matas Buzelis (Bulls), Alex Sarr (Wizards), Reed Sheppard (Rockets), Donovan Clingan (Trail Blazers), Zach Edey (Grizzlies) and Zaccharie Risacher (Mavericks).

stories.title: Dumonts take over as controlling owners of Mavericks
stories.summary: Sivan and Patrick Dumont purchased Miriam Adelson's shares of the Mavericks last month, making the Dumont family the controlling owners of the franchise.
stories.detailText: Sivan and Patrick Dumont purchased Miriam Adelson's shares of the Dallas Mavericks last month, making the Dumont family the controlling owners of the franchise with a 69% share. Adelson has had minimal involvement with the Mavericks since she bought the majority share of the franchise from Mark Cuban in December 2023 along with her daughter and son-in-law. Patrick Dumont has served as the Mavericks' governor since the families took control of the franchise. "It's really about long-term investment in the city of Dallas," Dumont told ESPN on Tuesday. "The Dumont family is really committed to building what we hope is the best arena in the NBA, a really significant investment in the city that will help create the new 40-year home for the Dallas Mavericks, a great experience for our fans and inspire our team to win championships. That's really what we're focused on. We had the opportunity, and we're really excited about it." Cuban, who has expressed regret about selling the Mavericks to Adelson and the Dumonts due to being frozen out of the franchise's basketball and business operations, maintains a 27% share of the franchise. According to the terms of the 2023 sale, Dumont can purchase another 20% share from Cuban at the original $3.5 billion valuation. "Our plan is to look at that and to do that over time," Dumont said. "I just have to tell you: I love Mark. He's been a great family friend for a really long time. He's just a super passionate Mavs fan and he's frustrated. I respect it. We're going to hopefully do him proud. That's my goal -- to make all of our Mavs fans super proud about the success of the team and win a championship." Dumont, the Las Vegas Sands Co. CEO, has overseen a major overhaul of the franchise during his turbulent tenure as the Mavericks governor. Dumont drew intense wrath from the fanbase for approving former general manager Nico Harrison's decision to trade perennial MVP candidate Luka Doncic to the Los Angeles Lakers months after the Mavericks' run to the 2024 NBA Finals. Dumont has since taken drastic measures to attempt to position the franchise for success as it pivots to build around Cooper Flagg , the reigning Rookie of the Year who Dallas drafted with the No. 1 overall pick after a historic stroke of lottery luck. "The most important thing every day is just trying to work harder to get better," Dumont said. "It's something that really applies in life, but it's something that really applies to here. It's been an experience as a new owner in the league. Dallas is a great sports city. I think we have the best fans in the NBA, very passionate, and it's my job to make sure that we win and that we support our fans. I'm really focused on that. I've learned that there are a lot of things you can do -- sometimes they work, sometimes they don't -- but you've got to keep pushing, got to keep going." Dumont, who fired Harrison last November, hired championship-proven former Toronto Raptors executive Masai Ujiri as president in May and authorized Ujiri to make sweeping changes throughout the front office and coaching staff. "This is Masai Ujiri's team," Dumont said. "He's got a ring. He knows what he's doing." Ujiri parted ways with former coach Jason Kidd and replaced him with Dusty May, who had just led Michigan to a national championship. Ujiri also hired general manager Mike Schmitz, who had been the assistant general manager for the Portland Trail Blazers . "I'm really proud of our team," Dumont said. "I think it starts on the basketball side with Masai Ujiri. He's a supreme talent. He's a great person with very high character. He works very hard. He's very focused on accountability and creating a winning team and creating a culture of success. It started with him." Dumont has also made hires in eight of the 11 senior leadership positions in the franchise's business operations over the last two years. Dumont recruited Naismith Hall of Fame executive Rick Welts out of retirement, hiring Welts in 2025 as CEO to help guide the franchise through a significant transformation, including planning for a new arena to open in 2031. Welts plans to retire again at the end of the calendar year and will be succeed by team president Ethan Casson, who joined the Mavericks in August 2025 after a nine-year tenure as the CEO of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx . "I've seen this movie before," said Welts, who led the Chase Center project during his decade-long tenure with the Golden State Warriors during that franchise's dynasty era. "I can't guarantee championships, but this [franchise] is destined for great success because of the leadership that Patrick has put in place on the business and basketball sides." The Mavericks' practice facility underwent an offseason renovation with at an eight-figure cost. A highlight of the renovation was the re-design and expansion of the dining area, creating the Champions Performance Kitchen in collaboration with the 50 Eggs Hospitality Group, providing players, coaches and staff an elite restaurant-caliber culinary experience and personalized performance nutrition. The team's business offices are currently undergoing an eight-figure renovation. The anticipation is that the franchise will have a new business office and practice facility when the Mavericks' new arena is scheduled to open in five years. The franchise entered into an option agreement this summer to purchase a 104-acre tract at the former Valley View Mall site in north Dallas, and the process of re-zoning to allow for the construction of an arena at that site is underway. "I'm feeling great about where we are in terms of creating the best building ever created for basketball," Welts said. "From a design perspective, we're way ahead of schedule. Patrick is very involved in that. Patrick has taken it to a different level. Patrick's interest in all things related to hospitality is unlike anything I've ever seen before. He builds the best hotels and resorts in the world. That's his day job, understanding how to build a premium hospitality experience. He's more involved in the building of this arena than any owner I can imagine." Dumont oversaw the construction of the Venetian Arena in Macao, China, which is two years into a five-year deal to host the NBA's preseason China Games. That building is a 12,000-seat arena with elements of a luxury resort. Dumont's plan is incorporate similar luxury touches into a larger arena with Texas style elements in Dallas. "That was something we couldn't do to the scale that we can do in Dallas," Dumont said. "I think what we bring to Dallas is going to be world class. My goal is to make the best arena in the NBA. It starts with the court and expands outwards, and I want to make sure the fans have the best experience possible, because we owe it to them."

The former Arizona Wildcats wing has signed a two-year deal with the Oklahoma City Thunder, according to ESPN’s Shams Charania. The contract comes at a good time for both sides: Terry was without an NBA team after getting by the Golden State Warriors in the preseason, and the Thunder are in need for an athletic swingman after suffering multiple injuries. Terry is on his third NBA team after playing the first four-plus years of his career with the Chicago Bulls before getting traded to the Philadelphia 76ers. In 218 career games, Terry is averaging 3.5 points, 1.7 rebounds, 1.2 assists and o.5 steals per game. The 6-foot-6 Terry arrives in Oklahoma City following injuries to the Thunder’s Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace . The Thunder are also without big man Chet Holmgren for at least two months. Terry was drafted 18th overall by Chicago in the 2022 NBA Draft. He comes the 17th former Arizona basketball player to be on an NBA team this season, the third-most of any school behind Kentucky and Duke.

stories.title: Karabell's notebook: Gobert's slow start, Zion's steals, and five other nuggets
stories.summary: Eric Karabell empties out the notebook with all that he's noticing around the NBA and what it means for fantasy.
stories.detailText: Part of the reason I invested in Minnesota Timberwolves C Rudy Gobert in a longtime dynasty league -- and this year in a shallower format -- was so that I would not have to deal with uncertainty. Gobert is 34 years old and has been doing the same thing statistically for more than a decade. He rebounds, blocks shots and converts the field goals he attempts, and few are consistently better at this. You don't draft Gobert for assists or free throw shooting. You know what you're getting. With some fantasy options, I don't want to be surprised. Perform as expected, please. The Gobert we have seen so far this season is not playing to form. He recently missed all 13 field goal attempts over a two-game span, he has blocked four shots in seven games and, while nobody thought he would be Stephen Curry from the free throw line, I was hoping Gobert would make more than half his attempts and wouldn't be forced to attempt so many. (He was an excruciating 4-for-12 on Monday!) Gobert even attempted a pair of 3-pointers in a recent game. He entered this season 0-for-22 in his career. Gobert is relatively durable, having played 70 or more games for four consecutive seasons. Then he missed a weekend game. I wasn't even mad. My shooting percentages went up. Don't drop Gobert, of course, but also don't trade for him as if everything will fall into place like, well, every previous season. Perhaps the back injury that cost him a game explains the brutal shooting, which includes myriad missed layups. It's only a few weeks, after all. Gobert sure wasn't too old last season when he led the NBA by hitting 68.2% of his field goals, averaged a double-double in points and boards for the 10th consecutive season and earned a spot on the All-Defensive team for the ninth time. In other words, while there has been some hint of regression in his formidable game in recent seasons, it was hardly to this level. For our purposes in fantasy, Gobert isn't a fantasy building block, but he averaged 33 ESPN fantasy points per game last season. He was easily a top-100 player, and better in roto/categories formats, where the stats he dominates stand out more than his deficiencies. He was a reasonable top-75 selection in ESPN drafts. He isn't playing that way so far, averaging a mere 19.6 FPPG. That's not cool. Fantasy managers tend to blame themselves when they finally invest in the "safe player" and, suddenly the player picks that season to sputter and not be safe. Is that Gobert? I will try to be patient here. Other observations around the NBA Speaking of free throws, how did New York Knicks SF/SG Mikal Bridges attempt zero through six games and 164 minutes? On Monday, Bridges finally went to the line, but he scored only six points in 16 minutes. Bridges is off to a brutal start, averaging 6.1 PPG and shooting 30.8% on field goals. While the valuable durability of literally never missing a contest is nice, I've generally viewed Bridges as a bit overrated in fantasy, certainly not worthy of a top-50 pick, but he averaged 33.3 fantasy points per game last season. This season: 13.9! Again, some patience is warranted, but I would be more patient with Gobert. Can I just admit how much I enjoy watching Cam Spencer ? The Memphis Grizzlies SG/PG, barely drafted in 2024, wasn't supposed to play much last season, but he averaged 11.1 PPG and 5.6 APG, with relevant 3-pointers and solid shooting, and he saved my dynasty league team (16 of 25 players start, so it is deep). I kept Spencer around. He started a weekend game with SG/PG Ty Jerome out and tallied 13 assists with nary a turnover. PG/SG Scotty Pippen Jr ., who I also liked, is off to a terrible start. OK, so Spencer may boast little upside, but I just want this fellow to get 20-25 MPG and not hurt my team. He isn't Jerome, one of the breakout options so far, but Spencer matters. I am not the fellow you come to for recommending New Orleans Pelicans PF/C Zion Williamson , but he deserves some credit for leading the league in steals entering this week. Where did that come from? Williamson had 60 steals in 62 games last season. He had 19 steals in his first six games, though he added none in Monday's overtime win. That's awesome, like Dyson Daniels stuff. Of course, until Monday, Williamson didn't have more than six rebounds in any game, and now he is averaging 5.3 RPG. That's just weird. I have no Zion shares, but I follow it all. I can't imagine someone coveting a player in a draft or trade who not only misses so many games, but his statistics when he does play are, well, inconsistent. I admit I may have acted hastily in ripping the fantasy value of Miami Heat C/PF Bam Adebayo in last week's column after barely a week of games. Adebayo scored 51 traditional points, with 18 rebounds and six steals, in recent games against the Atlanta Hawks and Indiana Pacers , and then he added 16 points and nine boards Monday at the Lakers. He fit in just fine with Giannis Antetokounmpo in those contests. Does that mean we sell high on Adebayo? Nah, not really. He has been more aggressive, and the Heat made more effort to get him involved. It worked. I don't see how PG Davion Mitchell can average 16 PPG and 8 APG all season, though. He would have to be a factor in the Most Improved Player competition. Perhaps? We don't do meaningless victory laps around here, but if you drafted Portland Trail Blazers PG Ja Morant , I must wonder, like, what did you expect? Morant is averaging only 15.8 PPG and 5.5 APG through four games, and he will not play his fifth for at least a month after suffering a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Morant appeared in 20 games last season, giving him 79 games over the past three seasons . Even Philadelphia 76ers C Joel Embiid played in more games during that span. The other difference is, Embiid produced elite numbers when he played. Morant did not. Now he's out until December, and it's not like we can count on him playing 80% of the games after that , either. Morant's generous projections and optimistic ADP shocked me. Who wants to deal with that in fantasy? Perhaps we see LA Clippers SF/PF Brandon Ingram as soon as next week. The former Laker, Pelican and Raptor is dealing with a partially torn Achilles, and there hasn't been great clarity on when he will make his season debut. Still, I stashed him in one league, thinking his value had fallen too far. Perhaps someone can play through a partially torn Achilles? I don't know! Still, Ingram has averaged at least 20.0 PPG in seven consecutive seasons, with at least 5.0 RPG and 5.0 APG annually, too. Durability is not a strength, but this Clippers team lacks scoring, and when Ingram plays, he should deliver numbers. Act now before Ingram (65.7% rostered) returns and starts producing his typical statistics, which may not be of the top-50 variety, but surely are top-100 worthy.

stories.title: NBA defends Rwanda partnership in letter to concerned senators
stories.summary: NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum cited the removal of a military-backed team from the Basketball Africa League as evidence the NBA has adapted to changing U.S. policies toward the East African nation.
stories.detailText: In response to two senators who called on the NBA to reevaluate a partnership with Rwanda and its dictator Paul Kagame, deputy commissioner Mark Tatum cited the removal of a military-backed team from the Basketball Africa League as evidence the NBA has adapted to changing U.S. policies toward the East African nation. In a letter directed to Sens. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., Tatum stated that after the U.S. imposed economic sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Force early this year, the military-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise team "was withdrawn" from the BAL. Tatum wrote that APR would remain "ineligible to compete in the BAL while these sanctions remain in effect." Tatum previously has said the NBA follows the lead of the U.S. government in deciding where it's "appropriate" to conduct business internationally. Merkley and Blackburn had written to NBA commissioner Adam Silver last week that they were "increasingly alarmed by the NBA's deepening relationship with Rwanda." In addition to asking the league to answer a question about APR, the Senators posed several other questions, including whether the NBA had a "red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses." Tatum didn't address that question or others directly. He wrote that, "Our mission is to inspire and connect people through basketball, both in the United States and more than 200 other countries and territories around the world where we engage with our fans. Our business around the world is not one-size-fits-all, but in all instances we follow U.S. policy in deciding where and how to operate. And we condemn human rights violations wherever they occur." Tatum concluded his letter by stating, "Going forward, we will continue to adjust to changed circumstances as U.S. policy requires." Kagame's government has been accused by the U.S., U.K. and other countries, as well as a string of human rights organizations, of abuses ranging from imprisonment, torture and murder of political opponents to the funding of child soldiers in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo. Last week, the U.S. government announced new sanctions on Rwanda over its ongoing support of the M23, a rebel group that Merkley and Blackburn said had "summarily executed hundreds of civilians, committed mass rape, recruited child soldiers, and tortured civilians" in the DRC. The same senators wrote Silver two years ago in response to an ESPN article that detailed the NBA's embrace of Kagame, the country's leader since 1994. Rwanda, one of the poorest countries in the world, built a 10,000-seat arena in its capital of Kigali, and that facility has been central to the NBA's expansion into Africa. Early last year, the DRC called on the NBA, Formula 1 and major international soccer clubs to end their multimillion-dollar partnerships with Rwanda. Months later, amid pressure from fans and media, Bayern Munich and Arsenal said they were ending their sponsorship deals with Rwanda.

stories.title: Phoenix is falling behind, and there’s no room for another slow start
stories.summary: A familiar record has brought a different reality, with higher expectations and no draft pick to fall back on.
stories.detailText: Nov 2, 2026; San Francisco, California, USA; Phoenix Suns guard Jalen Green (4) bites his shirt during a Golden State Warriors free throw during the third quarter at Chase Center. Mandatory Credit: Kelley L Cox-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There are plenty of things in life that give people anxiety. For me, it’s being late. Or even the threat of being late. Perhaps it’s the military man in me, somebody who made the mistake of showing up late to formation during basic training and paid for it in the front-leaning rest position, beads of sweat dripping off my nose and forming a puddle beneath me on the warm pavement at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, one June morning. If you’re not early, you’re late. That’s been my mantra ever since. Unfortunately, that familiar anxiety is beginning to build regarding the Phoenix Suns. This team is 12th in the Western Conference standings after starting 1-4, something we’ve seen before. At this point last season, the Suns were also 1-4 and were 13th. The difference then is they were only 3.0 games out of first, and due to an odd scheduling start for the Suns and the fact that they have played the fewest games in the NBA, they are 4.5 games back of the top team in the league. That team? The Rockets… These slow starts create a significant barrier between the Suns and a proverbial train that’s already leaving the station, headed toward the postseason. That’s right, the Suns are in danger of being late for that train. Anxiety! Because with every passing day and every loss that accumulates, they find themselves falling further and further behind, making it increasingly difficult to hop on board and reach their desired postseason destination. A season ago, we found ourselves in the same predicament, but the feeling surrounding the team was much different. A big part of that came down to expectations. Nobody really expected the Suns to be a team that could compete at a high level. The prevailing thought was to let the season play out, sell off assets around the trade deadline, and begin building toward the summer of 2026. Following that 1-4 start, the Suns began putting things together. The sloppy basketball we’d witnessed early in the season became more organized, and the effort that was evident through those first five games finally started translating into wins. I had this to say after they lost 114-113 to the Grizzlies a season ago: Losing still stings, but this team isn’t miles away. The execution needs tightening, and these are the aches that come with learning how to win again. It’s tough to find moral victories in Game 5 when you’re sitting at 1–4, but I’ll say it anyway. I was entertained. Disappointed, sure. The ending wasn’t what anyone wanted. But maybe this year isn’t about wins and losses. Maybe it’s about how they respond to nights like this. The feeling this year is different, however. Locally, expectations were higher, even if the national perception remained relatively unchanged. The roster construction was clunky, but you could at least see the vision of what this team wanted to become. Regardless, those expectations change the reality of your situation. While the effort has certainly been present, its consistency has begun to wane, and the execution remains frustratingly inconsistent. Last season, we could talk ourselves into believing thatDillon Brooks and Jalen Green’s absence due to injury was a significant reason for the team’s struggles. And perhaps this year, we’re doing the same thing with Mark Williams. But the feeling isn’t the same. The reality of the situation is slowly sinking in, and it’s one in which hope is becoming increasingly difficult to find. This is a team that doesn’t control its own draft picks, so finding itself stuck in the middle of the standings is essentially a death sentence. When you consider the anti-tanking rules that will be in place this year, there’s a very real possibility that the Suns could find themselves among the teams with an 8.1% chance of landing the number one overall pick. And how “Suns” would it be for Phoenix to benefit from not being completely horrendous under the league’s new draft lottery structure, only to have to hand that pick over to Houston? Are we there yet? Are we seriously thinking about this already? (I am) When you start 1-4 and look around the standings at the other teams with only one win, seeing the Kings, Nets, Jazz, Bulls, and Bucks alongside you, it’s difficult not to get a little frazzled. Because those are the teams that were projected to be bad. It’s why we’re running to the trade machine trying to find fixes, because you have no room for a down season when there is no benefit to being bad. I think back to a season ago and the turnaround we witnessed. What the Suns accomplished was impressive, climbing out of 13th place in the Western Conference and playing some incredibly good basketball along the way. For one fleeting night on January 22, 2026, the Suns had fought their way all the way back to the fifth seed in the Western Conference. After starting 1-4, they went 26-13 to reach that point. That is going to be incredibly hard to replicate. Can this team reproduce any aspect of what we witnessed last year? Can they put together another impressive run that allows them to hop aboard that train headed toward the postseason? There is hope if you look hard enough. Through their first 5 games a season ago, the Suns had a 120.5 defensive rating (28th) and -9.8 net rating (27th). This season, they are at 124.0 (30th) and -9.8 (25th). After their 1-4 start a season ago, the Suns posted a 112.3 defensive rating (8th) and a +2.1 net rating (13th). It is possible. We’ve seen it before. Psst…I’m saying the quiet part out loud…that team can rebound the damn ball…the worst team in rebound percentage last season was the Washington Wizards at 47.1%. The Suns are currently at 45.7%… We’ve got a long trip ahead of us, my fellow Suns fans, and we’ll spend much of that journey wondering whether this team can recapture any semblance of what it was a season ago. We’ll look for solutions in every corner, talking ourselves into the viability of overpaid players like Domantas Sabonis or Dejounte Murray as mediocre saviors. But with so many red flags surrounding the roster construction, it’s difficult to shake that familiar feeling of anxiety from being late building in the pit of your stomach.

(Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images After garnering considerable praise during the offseason and training camp for his development and diligent work, Adou Thiero has unfortunately yet to suit up in the regular season as he deals with swelling in his left knee. But according to head coach JJ Redick, it sounds like the second-year forward is potentially nearing a return. “He’s had some live exposures and I think he’s trending in the right direction,” Redick told reporters prior to the Los Angeles Lakers’ win over the Miami Heat on Monday. “Hopefully by the end of the week he’ll be available.” Thiero’s latest injury bout marks a turbulent first year and change in the NBA. He missed considerable time as a rookie with swelling in his left knee, which sidelined him for all of preseason and the first 13 games of the regular season, before a sprained MCL in his right knee rendered him unavailable from late December to mid-February. Fortunately, it sounds like he should be back sooner rather than later; although, swelling in the same knee a year later is undoubtedly concerning. His point-of-attack defense and general activity, both of which popped at times during the preseason , could help invigorate the Lakers’ 18th-ranked defense. They’ve often struggled to contain the ball and looked overmatched athletically on the perimeter at times. If he can find a reliable role offensively — and playing alongside Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves increases that possibility — Thiero’s size and athleticism can remedy some of those issues. For now, though, the focus is on Thiero becoming fully healthy and returning to the floor. Once he does that, determining whether there’s a spot for him in Los Angeles’ wing rotation, one that’s off to a pretty commendable start through eight games, can enter the conversation. In the meantime, Los Angeles will keep relying on Ziaire Williams, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia and Quentin Grimes to hold things down at the forward spots. The Lakers will look for their seventh win of the season when they face the Sacramento Kings inside Golden 1 Center Wednesday night at 7 p.m. You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: 'We don't have enough time to recover:' Is the NBA game outpacing the players?
stories.summary: Only two weeks into the season, the NBA has a growing injury problem.
stories.detailText: Standing near half-court with a towel draped over his shoulders, Thunder center Isaiah Hartenstein attempted to drum up encouragement for his rookie deputy Aday Mara as he approached the bench. Teammates Micah Peavy and Bennett Stirtz waited to do the same, while occasionally tilting their heads back at the jumbotron, which flashed a deficit of nearly 20 points. Veteran guard Alex Caruso, dressed in street clothes, could only clap his hands in hopes of bringing a jolt of energy that simply would not come in a 119-98 loss to the Rockets — an unimaginable, disheartening new normal. The 2026-27 season kicked off a fortnight ago, but Oklahoma City has already endured a campaign's worth of misfortune. Jalen Williams, lost to a fractured left fibula and a dislocated ankle . Cason Wallace, lost to a torn left labrum . Chet Holmgren, lost to a right patellar tendon tear . A tight-knit group that has always preached the importance of being where their feet are now is struggling to find its footing. A team that stood atop basketball's pinnacle less than 18 months ago now is dealing with questions about ever seriously challenging again, despite still boasting the reigning MVP and a former Coach of the Year. It's a unique type of hoops purgatory the organization hasn't experienced before. "The morale's been pretty good all things considered," coach Mark Daigneault said on Saturday. "A week ago, the circumstances were a lot different than they are today. We understand that. We try to have an approach that can transcend these circumstances and the guys have done a great job. Obviously, the challenge is a little different now than it was prior to those injuries, but we have to recalibrate to what the challenge is and attack it a day and a game at a time." While injuries have always been a part of the game, especially when competing at the highest level of the sport, the widespread volume and degree of ailments is troubling. One team being suddenly down 60% of its projected starting lineup is one thing, albeit a needle-in-a-haystack type probability. But the list of unavailables — Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Ja Morant, Ben Simmons, Jaren Jackson Jr., Paolo Banchero, Jalen Duren, Kawhi Leonard, Jalen Suggs and others — is growing, with various timelines ranging from multiple weeks to multiple months. Stars and teams are also being cautious with back-to-backs, whether due to early load management or having returned from long-term injuries. (The Pacers had 10 players out against the Hawks on Monday night, the second night of a back-to-back, citing a combination of rest and injury management.) But the games aren't slowing down for anyone. The season has become streamlined to some degree, with the shortening of training camp/preseason (the typical ramp-up period) and the insertion of the NBA Cup. It's clearly taken a toll on the players, which in turn takes a toll on the overall product. And there doesn't seem to be an immediate fix for cramming 82 games into a six-month schedule. Rockets are playing their seventh game in 11 days to start the season with two sets of back to backs. It is utter insanity. The schedule has become more condensed, which is bad for player health, because of the NBA Cup. Teams will play 2 games over an 11 day stretch in December — Adam Spolane (@AdamSpolane) November 1, 2026 Rockets guard Marcus Smart, who's dealt with serious injuries over his 12-year career, had an honest take on the growing epidemic. "The level of basketball has become so extreme on the human body and we don't have enough time to recover like we used to," Smart said. "When I first came in the league, training camp and preseason were damn near three weeks, multiple games to get your body ready for an 82-game season. Now, depending on how far you go in the playoffs, you might get two months off? It's tough on the body. "People don't understand; you're flying, your body's inflamed, you're landing in different time zones, go to sleep late and gotta be up early. Run as hard as you can, jump as high and fast as you can and be as physical as you can. All you're doing is asking yourself for injuries. But we signed up for it, and have to figure out a way to minimize it. Some of our best players are getting hurt and it's very unfortunate. We all want to be out here doing what we love." There is a long list of sports scientists, doctors, data analysts and professionals who will attempt to dissect such a rapid rise of injuries in a short amount of time. But simply watching every night, the games look more rigorous, more demanding and more taxing. Possessions are up , with the Chicago Bulls topping out at 110.2 a night, up from 107 courtesy of the 2025-26 Miami Heat. League average pace from the previous campaign is now hovering over the bottom third . The game has also become more aggressive. Last season's Pistons team, thought to be one of the more physical units around, committed 22 fouls per game. That same figure would rank 18th today . More teams are comfortable sending bodies to the offensive glass, with the Milwaukee Bucks' 33 chances per night a whopping 10 marks higher than last season's No. 1. On the defensive end, no team averaged double digits in contested rebound rate last season — there are eight such teams now . Average team speed and distance are up, too. It's a week into the season and the NBA is averaging the most possessions per game, shortest average possession length, highest average pickup distance, and most possessions with at least three offensive players crashing in the tracking era. Playing very hard for 82 games! https://t.co/knfp3i3VXq — Caitlin Cooper (@C2_Cooper) October 27, 2026 "There's not just one straightforward answer," said Jeff Stotts, injury analyst and owner of InStreetClothes.com . "I think you're seeing younger players get injured with a higher frequency because they're likely to have more miles on their legs before they get to the NBA. … I think the game has outpaced the player. And now you're asking your bigger, stronger athletes to also cover more ground, not only work on accelerators but also their brakes. Asking our big guys to stretch their games all the way out to the 3-point line. All those things increase the chances and likelihood of injuries occurring along the way." Last season, only three players averaged more than 36 minutes a night — Amen Thompson, Kevin Durant and Luka Dončić. That list has since nearly tripled in size. The aforementioned list of injured stars sans Haliburton also has another thing in common: all of their usage rates were lower than the previous season. What that means is while you may be on the ball less, you're off the ball more — relocating, cutting, changing direction and using your body in other ways that still can accumulate pressure and load. A good indicator of injury prevention is measuring an athlete's workload against their overall fitness level. Essentially the more they're asked to do physically, the more time they need to recover. "We're in this constant back and forth between rest and acute-to-chronic load ratio, where we're trying to minimize spikes," Stotts said. "Sudden increases in load on the body in relationship to the overall conditioning of the athlete. The teams that have found success have found ways to quantify the data in a way that helps buy-in. Some teams won't rest players; others will build it in. There's no great cure." Is such a spike in absences this early into the season enough to warrant an alternative look at scheduling or the larger umbrella of how the sport is played altogether? No magic wand can guarantee a clean bill of health, but the games, pace and aggression are increasing in frequency — and the players, whom the entire business model and ecosystem revolves around, are suffering because of it.

stories.title: How the Knicks' season, title defense got chaotic -- fast
stories.summary: New York has stayed in the headlines -- for all the wrong reasons. Can the 2026 champs bounce back?
stories.detailText: THE VISUAL WAS telling, if not stark. The Philadelphia 76ers moved the ball all over their NBA Cup-adorned court while the New York Knicks scrambled to catch up, reminiscent of how the reigning champions ran things in the second round of last season's playoffs when they won 15 of their final 16 games, including 13 straight. This time, the Knicks weren't taking over Xfinity Mobile Arena. They didn't get 3-pointers from Josh Hart or Miles McBride or Jalen Brunson after good ball movement. Instead, 76ers star Tyrese Maxey was driving down the lane for an easy dunk. Sixers fans chanted "MVP" for Maxey instead of being drowned out by their rivals who made the trek down I-95. LeBron James , after a tip-in that sealed the game, basked in the love as the newest addition to this rivalry. And after Philadelphia handed New York its fourth loss of the season ( 98-93 ) on Friday night, Hart carried a bloody bruise atop his freshly braided head. Heavy is the head that wears the crown. If "easy" was the word used to describe the Knicks' spring, they haven't had a moment of ease since. Off the court, the team has been plagued by headlines about contract extension talks being paused for its stars until season's end and a championship ring controversy. On the court, they've posted a 3-4 record, ranked 22nd in offense and shot 35.7% from 3-point range, slightly above league average. Early returns have the Knicks often looking like two different teams within the same night, sometimes the same quarter. Before, when the Knicks would go on one of those devastating runs of ball-popping offense and suffocating defense, teams would cower. You could feel it . Momentum building, an almost inevitable feeling that everything would eventually go the Knicks' way -- a massive factor in their record 14.9-point differential in the playoffs. Now, teams merely wait out the Knicks, knowing an opening is coming. "One thing I see, when we get those runs, we start to look like the team we've been in the past. [Then] we get a little comfortable," Brunson said following the Knicks' 111-102 loss to the Orlando Magic on Oct. 25. "We've got to continue to put our foot on the gas and execute like we did last year." Coach Mike Brown didn't deny his team has gotten off to a lethargic start. His task of getting this team to repeat as champions is tough enough: The parity era of eight champions in the past eight years is the longest such stretch in NBA history. Only last season's Thunder even made it out of the second round in pursuit of defending their title. It could be the competition catching up to the Knicks, or the uncertainty of player contracts having a very human effect. But to his credit, Brown is focusing on the long game and not the panic that can set in with a misfortunate start to the season. "This is a new season. It's a new team, and we're going to have challenges in front of us," Brown said. "It's like climbing a mountain. You know, sometimes you go 100 yards, but you might get knocked back 5 yards. "You regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way by making sure we embrace the process." IT'S NOT UNCOMMON to see Hart stewing after a bad game or a bad stretch. More than his buddy-cop relationship with Brunson, he is the emotional center of the Knicks and has been since he arrived in 2023 at the trade deadline. When the Knicks lost three straight games late last season, culminating in a 17-point road loss to the Rockets in Houston, Hart called it out, claiming the next night in Memphis was a must-win game. "We're not going in the right direction," he said that evening. The Knicks responded by winning the next five games before resting their regulars in the season finale, paving the way for their dominant playoff run. Hart doesn't mind saying the uncomfortable thing. But with his contract status up in the air, will he hesitate should an issue arise? "I guarantee you, I'm going to be sitting here rock bottom," Hart told ESPN. "I don't think I'm ever going to be on my high horse, either. "We're in New York. Everything rides on the next game. We go on a 10-game winning streak and the next game we lose, they're ready to burn the place down. We know what it is. It's the tough part of being in New York." Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla, whose team handed the Knicks their second loss of this season, understands how hard it is to move past a loss. "I don't think the psychological wars ever end after a game, I think it goes on for you as long as you're in it," Mazzulla said. "Every team brings in scars from the past." Brown has pointed to on-ball defense, indecision on offense and his players standing around when plays break down as culprits for the slow start. According to NBA.com, the Knicks trail only the Houston Rockets and Charlotte Hornets in frequency of shots late in the shot clock (four seconds or less), and shooting 28.8% in those situations ranks them behind only the Portland Trail Blazers in efficiency -- they were best in the league last season. Usually, that's Brunson time, as he did so often in the playoffs. But the magic hasn't been there to start the season. The Knicks haven't come back from big deficits the way they did last season, when they rallied from double-digits in six playoff games, the largest being a 29-point comeback over the San Antonio Spurs to win Game 4 of the Finals. Have they lulled themselves into a false sense of security with all those improbable comebacks? Will they dig themselves a hole too deep to emerge, and what's the cost of playing that way consistently? "I've said in the past it's important to learn from wins; obviously, you learn from losses as well," Brunson said Friday in Philadelphia. "There's been plenty of times we learned from being down what we can do. And in that same game, made adjustments to where we weren't down anymore. We have to put a full 48 minutes together." The 76ers, a team still building sweat equity after acquiring James and Jaylen Brown in the offseason, exposed what appears to be the Knicks' kryptonite: speed. "Sometimes it takes us a little longer to get into the game. Whether that's the flow, whether that's fatigue," Hart said. "Not relying on these comebacks because it's taxing. "We all feel the fatigue. We've got to fight through it. It's six games in, we've got to find a way to get our bodies ready to play. Mentally we're there; we've got find it physically." When Brunson was asked about it, he dismissed it flippantly: "Josh said he feels the fatigue? Josh is old as s---." It is not just Brunson and Hart who bear those scars. It took swingman Mikal Bridges four games before he connected on a 3-pointer, and seven games before he even attempted a free throw. Finals MVP Brunson is shooting at career-low marks from the field and from 3. And Brown is toggling between Andre Drummond and James Wiseman as backup centers in an effort to replace Mitchell Robinson , who signed a free agent deal with the Celtics when the cost-conscious Knicks failed to retain him. New York has felt the impact of losing Robinson, particularly in efficiency: He shot 72% from the field in 2025-26, while Drummond hit 47% last season and is shooting just 46% so far in this one. Wiseman is 0-for-5 from the field. McBride said it's not just up to Brunson and Hart to speak up; this team is self-aware and mature enough to have those hard conversations. "It's open," McBride told ESPN. "Anybody can step up, whether it's the [bench] guys or starters. That's the thing about this team, our chemistry is so good and we have a lot of trust because we see each other putting forth a lot of work." Brown, for his part, is not afraid to speak up, either. When the Knicks' season reached a breaking point last spring, down 2-1 to the Atlanta Hawks in the first round, Brown challenged Towns to get the ball more and be aggressive with it. It turned around their entire fortunes and led to their record playoff winning streak. "I'm going to keep it real," Brown said in early October. "If there's something in front of us, I'm not a fan of having an elephant in the room. I'll address it. I don't care if it's Jalen or KAT or OG [Anunoby]." The Knicks won't catch anyone off guard this time. And their 3-4 record has them ranked No. 8 in the East. Perhaps for his own sanity, Brown said he evaluates the season in five-game increments. Brunson believes the first month or so of games will be revealing. "I think everyone in the East knows each other," Towns told ESPN. "This is our third year now with each other, so you know, it's rare. That's one of our advantages." He compared it to James going to the Miami Heat in the summer of 2010 and how it changed the tone of the East for the entire decade. "At the end of the day, people knew, when LeBron and the big three were there, you had to go out there and beat them," Towns said. "Everyone brings their best against the New York Knicks. You've got to protect the jersey, the city at all costs." BROWN KEPT A steely face, giving nothing away when asked whether he had received his championship ring -- the latest in a string of less-than-flattering headlines since the team's title in June. It had been over a week since news broke that New York assistant coaches did not receive their championship rings on opening night. Additionally, some employees who had yet to receive their rings had been sent a phishing email from Madison Square Garden security that stated their "Employee Championship Ring is here." "I'm not going to talk about that ring stuff, as you can imagine," Brown said, despite speculation that the ring box he was handed was either empty or contained someone else's ring. "I'm not going to get into any of that." It's true to Brown's character. In his first year as Knicks coach, his gift was his ability to avoid making waves -- and lead the team to its first championship in 53 years, of course. Brown knows the path to another ring will be even harder. He saw it firsthand as an assistant coach with the Golden State Warriors , who added Kevin Durant to a team that had won 73 regular-season games the season before. The Warriors cruised through the playoffs in 2017, winning their first 15 games, but the next season they were nearly knocked out of the conference finals by the Rockets. And that was before the NBA's rules made it harder for teams to establish and maintain dominance. But even more telling is the fact that the teams that have repeated since the millennium have been headlined by James, Shaquille O'Neal , Kobe Bryant and Stephen Curry -- players on the short list of all-timers. Fittingly, Mazzulla understands the road Brown is journeying. After a 64-win season that culminated in a 16-3 run through the playoffs and the 2024 title, Mazzulla's Celtics followed it up with 61 wins in 2025, entering the playoffs as a defending champion many believed had a great chance at repeating. But they ran into the Knicks in the Eastern Conference semifinals, and the atrophy of the previous few seasons began to show. Jayson Tatum was the biggest casualty, tearing his right Achilles in Game 4 in New York as he desperately tried to get the Celtics back into a series they'd fallen behind in. "That's the competitive realm you're in. Once you're there, you have to trick yourself as if you've never been there," Mazzulla said. "But at the same time, two years away from that, every loss is more painful than it was three years ago. You have to treat yourself as if you're more desperate than everybody else." But the additional games add up, along with the breakneck pace of today's NBA. That has potentially played a part in the fate of the 2025 champion Thunder, who have four rotation players dealing with major injuries that could derail their season. Like Mazzulla's Celtics, who went to the Finals in 2022 before their breakthrough win in 2024, the Thunder have stacked multiple deep playoff runs -- a problem this Knicks team is also facing. Brunson has played 61 playoff games since coming to New York -- 37 in the past two seasons. Same for Hart. Anunoby joined the Knicks three years ago and has played 44 postseason games with the franchise and 71 overall dating back to his days in Toronto. Towns reached the conference finals in Minnesota the season before being traded to the Knicks, giving him 53 games over the past three postseasons. The bill on that could come due sooner than anyone expected. The Knicks are in contract limbo with three key players, after tabling all contract extension talks on Oct. 9. Owner James Dolan said this summer that New York wouldn't dip into the punitive second apron to keep the team together. Hart has a team option and on media day said there hadn't been any discussions on a new deal. Towns is eligible for a four-year, $276 million deal. Before talks were halted, the Knicks' offer was at $200 million , which represents a pay cut from his current salary (four years, $220.4 million). Towns hoped for a contract extension at the start of last season and didn't get it. The disappointment was quiet, but he played through an up-and-down regular season as he and Brown struggled to get on the same page; then it clicked in the postseason. He's prepared for a similar process. "I mean, we did it all last year," Towns told ESPN. "You're in New York, you've got to play through distractions; that's what comes with playing here. There's a lot of pressure, a lot of noise." "But as long as this locker room, which has shown it can do, stays together and continues to just believe and fall into each other when things get tough, we can do something special." Towns pointed to the Knicks' struggles after they won the NBA Cup last season, an ugly 2-9 stretch from Dec. 31 to Jan. 19, as proof they're built to handle adversity. "We didn't look our best version, and we heard about it," Towns said. "This team continued to fall into each other instead of splitting away and ... separating. We got closer and closer." In Philadelphia, Towns said: "We have to find a way to be that magical team we were last year. You don't want to wait to find that magic. Lightning don't strike twice."

stories.title: Bucks Reacts Survey: Are the Milwaukee Bucks too nice?
stories.summary: It’s hard to win games when you don’t strike any fear into your opponents. Right?
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 27: Kyle Kuzma #18 of the Milwaukee Bucks talks to Myles Turner #3 against the Philadelphia 76ers at Xfinity Mobile Arena on January 27, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The 76ers defeated the Bucks 139-122. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NBA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bucks fans and fans across the country. This Milwaukee Bucks season was never going to be pretty and, so far, well, the Bucks could crack mirrors. There’s still plenty to be excited about, of course—namely, the team’s three youngest players—but to this point these Bucks aren’t exactly the dawgs we hoped they’d be . Porous on the perimeter and feeble inside, are these Bucks simply too nice? Steal a possession? Deny a shot? Not these Bucks. After seven games, the Bucks have shown promise on the glass—even if there are some warning signs —in an attempt to win the possession game and maximise their opportunities to keep the scoreboard ticking over and the games close. But there is more than one way to skin a cat, and the Bucks aren’t doing much to make life difficult for their opponents—certainly not from a disruption point of view. So far, the Bucks sit dead last in steals per game (5.6 SPG), nearly half a steal worse than their nearest opponent (the Memphis Grizzlies, who average 6.0 SPG). They’re also dead last in opponent turnovers, forcing just 12.7 per game (nearly a full turnover fewer than the New York Knicks and Utah Jazz, who force 13.6 turnovers a night). All this means that Milwaukee isn’t generating extra looks through its defence. Compounding the issue, the Bucks are mediocre at best when it comes to turning back shot attempts. Myles Turner and (sometimes) Kel’el Ware aside, these Bucks simply do not block shots, averaging just 4.6 BPG thus far, “good” for 18th in the league. But the Bucks’ rim troubles don’t stop there. They’re currently 23rd in the league in defending the paint, conceding 50.9 points in the paint per night, while also allowing 27.6 free throw attempts per night (22nd in the league). It should come as no surprise then that they rank 21st in the league in opponent effective field goal percentage (at 54.8%). Roster limitations and mantra malfunctions Realistically, these numbers shouldn’t be too surprising. While Turner blocks shots, he’s never been an elite defender or physical presence—and he’s the Buck with the best defensive reputation. Kyle Kuzma and Jaime Jaquez Jr. compete, but they don’t have the physical gifts or explosive athleticism to be more than useful team defenders. In the backcourt, Tyler Herro has long been a defensive liability—or at least regarded as such. And none of these guys have any “nasty” in ’em. Ryan Rollins, on the other hand, has the length, and has shown the capacity to lock down at times. He’s also got some of that defensive stink to him (see his battles with Tyrese Haliburton). But in the early season, Rollins has seemed more intent on getting his shot off in a completely understandable bid to (1) prove himself worthy of the expectations placed on him prior to the season and (2) prove himself worthy of a new, lucrative contract—from Milwaukee or someone else—next offseason. Forest for the trees type stuff. Of course, it’s also worth noting that, despite their limitations, the starting group prior to last night’s change-up has actually been a real positive for the Bucks. This group—the team’s most frequent five-man lineup with 75 minutes of playing time—has a +21.6 net rating (per Basketball-Reference). Comparatively, just four of the team’s 19 other five-man lineups have fared better, but each of these have played fewer than seven minutes together. In fact, besides the starting group, no other five-man lineup has played more than 17 minutes of action thus far, making it difficult to truly determine which combinations are working and which aren’t. Another factor to consider is the team’s bench. Outside of AJ Green, the core reserves are all very young, meaning they’re simultaneously learning the NBA game and trying to establish themselves in the league. This is not a new combination, but it’s not an easy one either—and certainly not one that typically leads to winning basketball. Youth aside, the Bucks’ bench also lacks any true defensive aces—at least at this stage—despite their effort (see Kasparas Jakučionis, Brayden Burries, and Nate Ament) or gifts (see Kel’el Ware). All of this is to say that, like the players themselves, Jon Horst has more work to do. On a bigger scale, could the Bucks’ struggles to disrupt opposing offences in part boil down to a mantra malfunction? Their new motto, “Compete. Together. Get better,” sure is wholesome, but is it all a bit too Brady Bunch ? And is Jenkins leaning too much into relationship-building with his new herd of fawns? His decision to bench Rollins suggests not. The likely answer, then, is that this is simply a case of culture first, results later. Build rapport—nurture the youth— then let the metamorphoses begin. Regardless, for the Bucks to start doing more than show glimpses between the cracks, they might have to find a way to get a little meaner . What do you think? Are these Bucks too squeaky clean? stories.title: Q&A with Hall of Famer Mitch Richmond, talking Yaxel Lendeborg, LeBron, Jokic, Game Pulse
stories.summary: Richmond is NBA history personified and is still up on the modern game and players.
stories.detailText: Mitch Richmond is NBA history personified: NBA champion, Rookie of the Year, five-time All-NBA, six-time All-Star and Hall of Famer. For many fans, he is best remembered as part of the legendary Run TMC era of the Golden State Warriors, with Tim Hardaway and Chris Mullin. Before sitting down for an interview with NBC Sports, Richmond was interacting with fans on the NBA App through Game Pulse. For those unfamiliar, Game Pulse combines a live court visualization with highlights and advanced statistics, including shot charts, in a live-updating experience that also features commentary and perspectives from NBA legends such as Muggsy Bogues, Carlos Boozer, Gary Payton, Joakim Noah and more. Here is our conversation with Richmond (edited for length and clarity). NBC Sports: You've been on this Game Pulse NBA app experience with the fans. How has that been for you? Richmond: It's been great. You know, that's my first time being on the Pulse. I always watch the association, and sometimes I already catch everything on NBA TV. But it was my first time, so it was a good experience. Q: It seems like it's a good experience for the fans. They get real interaction not just with the studio people, but with people like yourself, who happen to be Hall of Famers. Richmond: Yeah, no question about it. It's just the fan engagement. The fans want to be as close as they can, and sometimes they want to hear from other players watching the game. So it gives me an opportunity to kind of reach out to them, and especially since I played so long ago, so they don't know me. But it's a time to start Googling me. You know what I mean? Q: I think people underestimate, though, like how great and how impactful Run TMC was, and that era of Warriors basketball. As you look at the league now. Is there a player that kind of reminds you of Tim Hardaway? Richmond: That's a good question. Oh man, who reminds me of Little Tim? Oh man, I don't, it's hard. He had such power when he dribbles the ball, he gives you that shoulder as he goes by that you can't get back in front of him. Yeah, man, that's hard to do. Q: It might be even harder with Chris Mullin in some ways. Richmond: Oh man, let's see who Mully would be. I mean, Mully was not the fastest guy, but it is back to what I say: It's how you use your body, and how you use your skills, and how you move. We see it now in today's game, it's all about getting guys in angles when they pick-and-roll. They want you on their back and they want to make sure that you never get back in front of them. Mully had the tendency, if you get on the side of him, he has a way that you never get back around him. And so he was really, really methodical of how he's going to move and take his little steps, and might do a little bird flip. So yeah, he was very tough to guard. Q: You're close to the Warriors still to this day. They've been fun to watch at the start of the season. What's impressed you about Yaxel Lendeborg as a rookie, just coming in like this? Richmond: Coming in with that attitude, man, like I belong. And truly, truly, they need a spark like that. We don't know how long Curry is gonna Curry is gonna give us, but they need a young star to come in and kind of help some of that load for Curry right now. I think he's the guy. He has the temperament, and I like him. I like how he came in with Luka, arguing a little bit, but hey, I think that you need that. You need that spark. You need that spice. Q: I like that [Warriors coach Steve] Kerr trusted him enough to give him that assignment in his first NBA game. Richmond: I'm pretty sure he wanted it, and I think that's what great players do at times, man. It's for greatness. I want to guard the best player. You know what I mean. I have no problem. I want to guard the best player. We haven't seen that in a while. Q: What other rookies have stood out to you? Richmond: I mean, you look at Caleb. Man, he's going to be a star down in Chicago. Caleb Williams. I like AJ [Dybantsa of the Wizards]. AJ is good. Even the young [Cameron] Boozer. Hopefully, he can start to get his game rolling. But I think it's a lot of good young talent that we have, and I just love watching the games, to tell you the truth. Q: Houston is off to a fast start. Dallas has knocked off two undefeated teams. What are you liking about those teams? What have you seen from them that's making them look kind of dangerous early? Richmond: I spent a little time with them in Macau when the Rockets played the Dallas Mavericks over there [preseason], and so they looked like just a fun team. And actually, both teams was personable, and I think they get along with one another. One, and they got two good coaches that's coaching them right now. So, man, I thought Houston had a little bit more than Dallas, but Dallas has been playing excellent this year. Q: Houston, I like the way they're built. I think they can be really dangerous in a West that feels a little more open right now. Richmond: No question about it. I think the West is wide open. I think someone... can Portland come out of there? You know Portland is looking pretty good right now. I think the West, like you say, the West is wide open. Lakers are even looking pretty good. Q: You mentioned Portland. Is there anybody else who's just like, wow! When they're on, I kind of want to watch them. I want to watch those players. Richmond: I'm loving watching the Knicks, tell you the truth. I love watching the Knicks and how they play. Then I just start going for players to see how they're doing. I go and pop over at Denver and see what [Nikola] Jokic is doing. I'm always on the channel with Golden State. I'm always turning the channel to Dallas. I mean, the Lakers, because the Lakers can actually do something as well. We didn't expect that, but the center that they got from Utah? Q: Walker Kessler. Richmond: I mean, no one ever saw this, buried in Utah, and now seeing him, and he was hurt as well. But to see what he's been doing and the numbers he's been putting up, you know, they needed a big man like that to run the floor and catch it at the rim. Q: On the other side, the Heat have just not gelled yet. It hasn't come together consistently. When you see them, what's missing? Richmond: I think just a little bit more time together. You know what I mean? I think sometimes, teams mesh very well. Look at Philly. You know, how LeBron [James] just came and and haven't missed the beat over there. They're just playing real fluid ball as well. I think Boston is playing pretty good as well. I think sometimes you need just a little bit more time to gel. We haven't seen that yet, so hopefully they can they can catch a groove and start winning some games. Q: Philadelphia has gelled really quickly, but is that just LeBron bringing his own culture and that's a team where guys seem willing to sacrifice, and they're kind of in the right place to make plays. Richmond: I think the sacrifice is a little different when you have a star player coming in that is a volume shooter. LeBron kind of plays every part of the game, so he doesn't need those 40-point nights. You know, he might have one this year, but he has enough guns around him. And I think the guys, you have your shooting hands ready to shoot the ball when you have a guy that is a willing passer, and LeBron has been more of a willing passer, especially when he knows that he got young guns at his beck and call anywhere he goes. These guys can really shoot the ball. Look at Embiid. Embiid is in better shape. The guys are bringing enthusiasm. They had some enthusiasm over there. Let's see if they can keep it the whole year, because at some point in time, teams are going to start figuring them out, and see how it happens. But I do like the start of them; they look like a team to be reckoned with later. Q: You mentioned Jokic's passing and a couple other guys. There are some great passers in the league right now. Who are some of the guys you want to tune in to watch because they see the court differently? Richmond: Jokic is that guy. You know, if I played with him, man, I'd be coming off screens all day, going back door because he truly, truly finds guys. We have to put LeBron, he's still there. LeBron still knows how to get passes to the right guys. It's a few others out there, but I just love how guys like that move the ball, share it, and it looks wonderful.

stories.title: Steph Curry’s historic streak ends at worst possible time in Warriors thriller
stories.summary: In a game that he finished with 33 total — his third in a row with 30 or more — it was the point Curry left on the board that left everyone talking.
stories.detailText: SAN FRANCISCO — Stephen Curry had stepped to the foul line 50 times this season with the same result. Swish. Bottom of the net. Put a point on the board. So, when he was fouled with the Warriors leading by two and less than six seconds left Monday night against the Suns, the game had to be as good as over … right? Well, eventually. Only after Curry clanked a free throw for the first time this season. Dillon Brooks grabbed the rebound and passed it ahead to Collin Gillespie, who got off a last-second heave from 36 feet. It was a clean look, albeit an unlikely one, and could have sent the game to overtime. The shot fell short and Curry’s ill-timed miss proved insignificant. Stephen Curry of the Golden State Warriors looks on during a game against the Phoenix Suns on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at Chase Center in San Francisco. NBAE via Getty Images But in a game that he finished with 34 total — his third in a row with 30 or more — it was the one point Curry left on the board that drew the attention. “I mean, he’s just made so many big free throws in his career,” coach Steve Kerr said. “Obviously he makes all of those. The law of averages catches up every once in a while.” Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry (30) shoots against the Phoenix Suns in an NBA basketball game in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn In addition to being the greatest 3-point shooter in history, it would make sense then that Curry keeps the same standard in a controlled setting, 8 feet, 9 inches closer to the basket. His 91.3% career rate makes him the most efficient foul shooter of all time. Curry is also responsible for two of the NBA’s four longest stretches of success from the stripe to begin a season. With his streak, he was closing in on himself (52 in a row in 2017-18) for third place and Steve Nash (53 in 2007-08) for second for the most foul shots without a miss. It would have taken some time to snatch the record away from Jose Calderon (84 in 2008-09). But with a chance to put the game on ice and move into a tie for third place, for the first time in a competitive game in 204 days, Curry’s shot clanked off the rim, into the hands of Brooks. Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry shoots against Phoenix Suns guard Devin Booker and center Khaman Maluach in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn Fortunately for the Warriors, the 11 free throws, five 3s and four shots inside the arc that did find the bottom of the net proved to be just enough in the 116-113 win, their fifth in a row. While Curry’s free throw streak came to an end at 51, he also extended another with his 34-point performance. At age 38 and 233 days, only two older players in NBA history have dropped 30 three games in a row: LeBron James and Michael Jordan . One miss in a vast ocean of splashes, of course, did nothing to shake Curry’s confidence. “I’m shocked,” Curry smirked, “when I miss anytime.”

stories.title: Thunder sign Dalen Terry out of G League to provide depth at forward
stories.summary: Terry, the No. 18 pick in the 2022 NBA Draft, played for the Bulls and 76ers.
stories.detailText: Needing perimeter depth after a series of injuries, the Oklahoma City Thunder reached into the G League and signed Dalen Terry of the Santa Cruz Warriors to a standard two-year contract, although the second year is non-guaranteed, a story broken by ESPN’s Shams Charania and confirmed by other reports . Terry, a 6'6" defense-first wing, was the No. 18 pick in the 2022 NBA Draft out of Arizona. He played three-and-a-half seasons with Chicago before being traded at last February's deadline to New York, which flipped him to New Orleans, and then the Pelicans waived him. Terry then signed a two-way deal with the 76ers and was promoted to a standard contract at the end of last season, but was waived to make room on the roster so the team could acquire LeBron James. Terry was in training camp with the Golden State Warriors and was set to report to their G League affiliate when the Thunder called. Across 218 NBA games, Terry has averaged 3.5 points per game. The positive spin for Thunder fans, and why the team took a chance on him, is that he is a plus defender on the wing whose 3-point shooting has improved each season, hitting 36.4% overall last season. Bringing in Terry helps the Thunder with depth in two ways. First, while he is not going to play a significant role, Terry can give them some wing minutes. Plus, by filling the 15th spot on the roster, the Thunder can use their two-way players without the restrictions of the "under-15" rule. The Thunder are without three starters due to significant injuries. All-NBA wing Jalen Williams is out with a fractured fibula and dislocated ankle, while All-Defense guard Cason Wallace is dealing with a torn labrum. There is no timetable for either player, but if they return at all this season, it will be late in the campaign. The Thunder also are without All-NBA big man Chet Holmgren due to a right knee patellar tear, but he is expected to return sometime after Christmas (likely in early 2027). The Thunder calmed the waters around them last night with a 117-112 win over the Cavaliers behind a big night from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. stories.title: Luka Doncic reveals intentions for off-day after another 40-burger in Lakers win
stories.summary: Luka Doncic is ballin' right now, and has his sights set on another sport.
stories.detailText: Luka Doncic was proud of the Lakers’ performance thus far this week. “It’s not bad. Now we got two wins in a row right here, so it’s a great start,” he said. Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers dribbles the ball during the game against the Miami Heat on November 2, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NBAE via Getty Images Doncic then added what he planned to do after the Lakers improved to 6-2 with a win over the Heat Monday night. “Play some golf,” Doncic said with a smirk as he walked through the tunnel after Los Angeles’ 138-117 win over the Heat on Monday. The Lakers superstar has become enamored with the sport, going as far as installing a golf simulator in his home. Doncic credits former teammate LeBron James and Austin Reaves as key influences in his golf game. Now, it appears the green is all the 27-year-old can think about after a great start to the week on the court. In the victory over Miami, Doncic finished the night with 42 points , 13 assists, seven rebounds and two steals. It marked the fourth time in the last five games that Doncic scored at least 40 points. By halftime Monday night, the Lakers superstar already had 24 points, making Doncic the first Lakers player to score at least 20 points in the first half in five consecutive games since Kobe Bryant in 2007. Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers celebrates during the game against the Miami Heat on November 2, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NBAE via Getty Images Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers dribbles the ball during the game against the Miami Heat on November 2, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NBAE via Getty Images The Lakers offense roared against the Heat, with arguably the unit’s greatest showing of the 2026-27 campaign. The squad finished with a season-high 138 points, putting the finishing touches on a historic Doncic performance. The Lakers superstar seems ready for his next challenge, only this time off the court and on the course.
